newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Philips marketing strategy seen key to success.
newsitem.headline: Philips marketing strategy seen key to success.

text.p: Philips Electronics has a unique chance to forge ahead with a global strategy based on the strength of its brand, convincing investors it can boost profits by selling more goods as well as by cutting costs, analysts say.
Speculation is growing about the approach to be taken by Gerard Dufour, the man appointed as senior director of marketing last October who has yet to make an overt strategy announcement.
Cor Boonstra, who took up the chairmanship last October, is credited with getting a grip on costs but many wonder how Philips will take the initiative and drive profits ahead.

Dufour sits at the head of a marketing organisation which over the last two years has slashed back a network of around 40 advertising agencies to just two, and industry watchers say that gives him and Philips big options to shape the firm's destiny.
Martin Jones, managing director of advertising consultants Advertising Agency Register, said the structure was bold and part of a dynamic emerging in world advertising markets.

"It says control. Your brand is the most important thing for your company, therefore the more control you have over it the better. If you've got 40-odd people looking after a brand, its tone of voice, there's more likelihood of you losing control of the centre than if you've only got two," Jones said.

Teetering on the brink of bankruptcy after stinging losses in the early 1990s Philips was nursed back to health by former chairman Jan Timmer, only to stumble back into a 590 million guilder net loss in 1996, the victim of persistent price erosion and market pressures.

Industry observers say Philips' brand perception as "worthy" or "solid" or "high quality but not quite leading edge" has obviously not helped it perform to its potential in intensely competitive markets, although financial markets have warmed to Boonstra's initial actions.

And lack of focus has been seen as a problem as Philips markets a product range that runs into a multitude of lines, from electric shavers and toasters to televisions, semiconductors and car navigation systems.

Boonstra's policy of getting rid of the "bleeders" -- the underperformers and non-core businesses -- has won a huge vote of confidence from investors who have driven Philips' share price to a recent record 120.80 guilders compared to 45.50 guilders barely a year ago.

But analysts say Philips is seen as a recovery stock and that any improvement from a low base is bound to look spectacular. They all avidly await an expected strategy statement from Boonstra who says a review of Philips' operations and business governance needs to come first.

Some might argue that Boonstra, an outsider who joined Philips in 1994 with a reputation as being a strong marketing man, has already flagged his strategy by appointing Dufour - the man behind Philips' "Let's make things better" slogan.

"It's pretty evident that the arrival of Mr. Dufour and the consolidation of all of the Philips advertising in two agency networks is an indicator that this (marketing) is an area which will take higher priority," said John Leonard, Executive Vice President Euro RSCG, Dufour's previous company, and one of the agencies retained by Philips.
Advertising specialists say globalisation of brands such as IBM, Coca Cola and Unilever is an identifiable trend and that Philips has the raw material to bestride the globe.
"Marketing is a global effort today and I think that you need to choose global partners with which to do it," said Leonard. "I think it's a general trend in marketing."

Philips has the qualifications to hold its own with the other heavyweights in its class, given its hundred-year history in which it invented the audio cassette and jointly developed the hugely successful audio compact disc.

No-one questions that Philips has the quality of design or technology needed to innovate and develop products but many wonder whether the company can prove it knows what its customers want and knows how to give it to them.

"A streamlining of the organisation is probably healthy but one needs to be sure that they really do know what the market thinks of its products and what the market needs from its products. And it's got to do something about both its products and the way it communicates," said one advertising man who declined to be named.
Timing, along with the shrewd marketing skills the world might expect from a global market player, will also be the key if Philips' new products are to compete in the market-place.

"In today's world so much has to do with timing. A brilliant idea in a slightly wrong time and you can be in trouble," said Leonard. "All these products for the future are products where Philips will be there along with the main competitors."
And if campaigns are won by lucky generals Dufour might have got off on the right foot by arriving at Philips at a time when marketing tools such as the Internet are gaining momentum.

"He's arriving at the right time, with the right brand. He's going to have the advantage of new media distribution systems, the Internet and database management. One will soon be able to know exactly who your consumers are and that allows you an awful lot of control," said Jones.
